paper_title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training [5, 14, 37, 71, 73] improves text rendering [37], compositional accuracy [19, 23] and human preference scores [26, 41, 66, 69] in image and video diffusion transformers [6, 13, 63]. These improvements are typically obtained by updating the models weights, either through parameter-efficient adapters such as LoRA [22] or through full fine-tuning [71]. Although the update is fixed after training, the updated weights 1 Figure 2 The steering vectors add the same vector to every token of every prompt. Block ℓ on two text-rendering prompts, with linear layer W, token inputs zi and zj, and block outputs hi and hj. Base + adds the same (black) to every token of both prompts; changes only with the block, guidance pass, step bin and stream. In the RL-tuned model, the weight change gives each input its own shift, Wzi = Wzj (gray). In block ℓ, is one vector and matrix: on SD3.5-M, all 188 vectors together hold 0.29M parameters, 65 fewer than the RL-tuned LoRAs 18.8M. + act on each tokens input, so different prompts and tokens produce different activation changes. This flexibility seems natural for visual generation, where the words to render and the objects to compose change with every prompt. But is this input dependence actually necessary to obtain the gains of RL post-training? Surprisingly, we find that most of the reward improvement of diverse collection of RL-tuned image and video generators can be reproduced by freezing every pretrained weight and adding small set of fixed steering vectors to the models activations. We fit these vectors to match the velocity predictions of each RL-tuned model, with no reward in the objective; simply averaging the activation changes that RL induces recovers far less of the gain. For given RL-tuned model, the same vectors are used for every prompt, every sampling seed, and every token  (Fig. 2)  . In total, they have 1.5% of the parameters of rank-32 LoRA on SD3.5M, and they do not depend on the requested text, objects, or composition. Yet they can make the frozen generator render requested phrases, satisfy compositional constraints and improve preference scores much as its RL-tuned counterpart does (Figs. 1 and 5). On six RL-tuned image models spanning SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev, multiple RL algorithms, LoRA and full fine-tuning, and rewards including PickScore, HPSv2.1, OCR, and GenEval, these fixed activation shifts recover 90.096.3% of the RL reward gain. The result extends to video: on two RL-tuned video generators, the same intervention recovers 89.8% and 111.9% of the gain. We next ask whether RL can learn such constant shifts directly from the reward in diffusion transformers. We freeze the generator and run Flow-GRPO [37] with only the steering vectors trainable, starting from zero. The trained vectors reach 104.6% and 103.6% of the gains of the OCR-tuned and PickScore-tuned SD3.5-M models, so RL achieves both gains by learning only small set of constant vectors, without updating any pretrained weight. How can one constant intervention produce different improvements for different prompts? The steering vectors carry no prompt information, so the prompt-specific part of the change must come from the frozen generator. Inside the transformer, attention, normalization and MLP layers mix the constant vector with prompt-dependent representations, so its effect on the output can depend strongly on the prompt. On SD3.5-M, we trace how the shift reaches the image: through what image tokens read from text tokens in joint attention. When image tokens read the text keys and values of the unsteered base model instead, with everything else unchanged, most of the OCR and PickScore gains disappear. The same replacement removes most of the gains of the OCR-tuned and PickScore-tuned models, so the steering vectors and RL reach the image by the same route. The text stream, the conditional guidance pass and the early sampling steps carry most of the gain: vectors fitted to these parts alone, with 531 fewer parameters than the rank-32 LoRA, recover 89.5% of the RL gain on OCR and 73.7% on PickScore (Sec. 5). These results suggest different view of RL post-training in visual generators: constant shift suffices to steer generation toward most of the RL gain, and the frozen generator does the prompt-specific work. Although RLs weight updates produce input-dependent activation changes, most of their reward gain is reproduced without new input-dependent transformations beyond those the base model already computes. Our main contributions are: We show that fixed steering vectors, fitted with no reward in the objective, recover most of the gain of eight RL-tuned image and video models, including two full fine-tunes. We find that matching the RL-tuned models velocity recovers far more of the gain than adding its average activation change. We train only the steering vectors of frozen SD3.5-M with Flow-GRPO and exceed the reward gains of the RLtuned OCR and PickScore models, with images rated on par with theirs in user study. We trace how constant shift yields prompt-specific gains: on SD3.5-M, it reaches the image through what image tokens read from text, as RLs change does. 2. Related work RL post-training of diffusion transformers. Reward finetuning raises score of diffusion models samples by backpropagating the score through the sampler [11, 51], by learning from preference pairs [62] or with policy gradients [5, 14]. Policy gradients [64] need only one score per sample, and their group-relative form in Flow-GRPO [37] and DanceGRPO [71] now post-trains image and video diffusion transformers [6, 13, 63]. The rewards include OCR accuracy [37], GenEval [19] and T2I-CompBench [23] scores, and preference models trained on human judgments [10, 26, 41, 66, 69]. Other studies report side effects on color saturation [45] and output diversity [3]. We ask what RL changes inside the model to produce these gains. Where RL acts. Studies of RL in language models ask where its update sits. RL fine-tuning updates small subnetwork [44], reaches most of its gain with few trained parameters [43] and keeps the model close to the base model [52]. Alignment tuning mainly changes the stylistic or first tokens of each answer [34, 48], and RL raises the probability of answers that the base model already samples [72]. Venhoff et al. [61] close most of the gap to RL-trained reasoning models with classifier-gated steering vectors: classifier decides where to add each reasoning behavior. Sinii et al. [54, 55] train steering vectors with RL on math reward and match or nearly match full RL fine-tuning, and Vakada et al. [60] do the same with label-free rewards. We fit ours to given RL-tuned model to measure how much of its gain constant recovers, and also train them with the reward (Sec. 4.6). We study diffusion transformers, in which reward gain is prompt-specific change of whole image or video. Activation steering. Activation steering adds fixed vector to models hidden states, taken from contrasting prompts [31, 49, 58, 74] or optimized [8, 56]. In image models, fixed direction in deep features edits image content [59], and similar, often gated, additions steer diffusion models [15, 29] and diffusion transformers [27]. Task arithmetic [25] adds the weight difference of fine-tuned model, which is constant in weight space but changes the activations of each input differently. In concurrent work, First-Order Steering [28] turns such weight update into steering vectors to first order. Adila et al. [1] find the block output, where our steering vectors sit, an expressive place for such shifts. We instead fit steering vectors to the velocity predictions of given RL-tuned model. Constants in network. Many adaptation methods change frozen model through parameters that are the same for every input. At the input, prompt tuning [30] trains soft prompt tokens, textual inversion [16] fits word for new concept and ReNeg [32] learns negative embedding on reward. RaTE [9] fits one prompt token to Flow-GRPO model by flow matching. Inside the network, prefix tuning [33] and P-Tuning v2 [39] prepend learned keys and values to attention layers, and ReFT [67] learns interventions on hidden representations. BitFit [4] and (IA)3 [36] train biases and channel scales, DiffFit [68] tunes the biases and scales of diffusion transformer and Calibri [57] tunes the block gates of diffusion transformers on reward. BitFit and DiffFit train biases with the task loss to adapt model to new data, whereas we fit steering vectors at the block outputs to an existing RL-tuned model to measure how much of its gain they reproduce. 3. Conclusion RL post-training updates the weights of diffusion transformer, so it changes the activations differently for each prompt and token, as prompt-specific skills such as text rendering seem to require. Yet steering vectors shared across all inputs and fitted with no reward in the objective recover most of the reward gain of six image and two video RL-tuned models. Fitting recipe Table S1 gives all fitting hyperparameters and the fitting cost. Every fit uses AdamW with betas (0.9, 0.999), eps 108, no weight decay and gradient clipping at norm 1, with one training seed. It starts at smean, measured on 256 calibration prompts. The training prompts are those of Flow-GRPO [37] on SD3.5-M and FLUX.1-dev, of GenRL [18] on Wan2.1, and of the public VBVR-Pro RL training set [70] on Wan2.25B. On SD3.5-M, the calibration and validation prompts come from the same training files. The learning rate rises linearly over the first 50 updates and stays constant until its decay. For the OCR-tuned and GenEval-tuned models, the checkpoint at 3,000 updates comes before the decay. New training states re-noise final images at level drawn uniformly from the samplers 40 noise levels, with new noise at each update. Fixed training states re-noise each prompts final image once per contiguous range of levels, with fixed noise. Table S2 gives the training settings of the steering vectors that Flow-GRPO trains from zero (Sec. 4.6). Training length. On SD3.5-M, we choose the number of training updates for each RL-tuned model among the checkpoints at 1,500, 3,000 and 4,500 updates of one training run, by the reward gain on that RL-tuned models validation set. No choice uses the test sets. The fitting loss on held-out prompts, which uses no reward, is lowest at 4,500 updates for all four SD3.5-M RL-tuned models. Choosing the length by this loss keeps the length of the two PickScore-tuned models, and it changes the validation gain of the OCR-tuned and GenEval-tuned models by 0.011 [0.026, +0.004] and 0.021 [0.059, +0.017]. Steering-vector layouts. Table S3 gives the layout of the steering vectors on every base model. Step bins. The energy of an RL-tuned models average change to the block outputs is its squared norm summed over the sampling steps. The change is in units of the base models activation standard deviation on SD3.5-M and in raw units on FLUX.1-dev. Averaging the change within contiguous groups of sampling steps keeps part of this energy. After 1,500 training updates, the three PickScore gains span 0.006 points on 512 PickScore prompts (Fig. S1). The three OCR gains span 0.011 on 256 OCR prompts. Starting point. Zero initialization reaches nearly the same gain as initialization at smean on PickScore and OCR. On the PickScore test subset of 512 prompts, zero-initialized fit gains +1.34 against +1.36 for fit initialized at smean. On 256 OCR prompts, the zero-initialized fit on 10,000 training prompts gains +0.317 and the fit initialized at smean gains +0.324. The two OCR fits reach this gain with different vectors, which have cosine similarity 0.33. The fit initialized at smean keeps cosine similarity 0.97 with smean, and the change that training adds to it has cosine similarity 0.90 with the zero-initialized fit. All four fits use at most 1,500 training updates and one training seed. Prompt count. On OCR, 64 distinct training prompts suffice to fit the steering vectors (Fig. S1). Every fit in this ablation uses about 10,000 samples of the RL-tuned model, at most 1,500 training updates and one training seed. On 256 OCR prompts, fit initialized at smean on 256 training prompts keeps the full gain of fit on 10,000 prompts. fit on 64 prompts keeps 94% of that gain, and zero-initialized fit on 64 prompts keeps all of its own 10,000-prompt gain. Finding 2 of Sec. 5 removes most of the OCR-tuned models gain by replacing the text keys and values that its image queries read with those of the base model. If the steering vectors carry the change that RL makes to these keys and values, computing them with the steered base model should restore the gain. We therefore repeat the replacement on the OCR-tuned model, with the text keys and values computed by the base model plus the OCR steering vectors on the same noisy state, on the OCR test set of 1,018 prompts at one sampling seed. The OCR-tuned model then keeps 95.2% [91.9, 98.6] of its gain, against 26.4% [20.7, 31.6] with the keys and values of the unsteered base model.
